author: Ken Klippenstein

This Thanksgiving, I'm thankful for everything I _don't_ have that many
reporters do: advertisers to satisfy with clicks, awards committees to woo
with boring prestige pieces, and billionaire "philanthropists" to keep happy.

I don't have to go to cocktail parties to beg for scraps of D.C. gossip.
(Hell, I don't even have to live in Washington.) I'm not in the club, not on
the guest list, not everyone's cup of tea, and that's the way I like it.

Truth is, not being on any team isn't some brave choice I made. I was born
into it. I've joked that if a carnival swapped one of those "Guess my weight"
booths for a "Guess my ethnicity" one, my winnings could fund this newsletter
forever. Or, as internet user "snarqueduct" put it:

A fun paradox of being biracial (I'm half Salvadoran) is if you say you're one
race, you're often told you're not _really_ one of them; but say you're the
other, and suddenly you're labeled "self-hating."

I like to joke that I'm against racism because a race war wouldn't go well for
me.

The upside of being ethnically ambiguous is that you get comfortable with
ambiguity, and with being ostracized for silly reasons. I never realized how
well that would prepare me for journalism.

This week serves as a nice illustration of what I mean.

On Tuesday, [I reported](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/jensen-huang-spy-
story-is-a-hoax) that the intelligence community never actually concluded that
Alice Huang, mistress of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, was a Chinese spy -- a hoax
propagated by Marco Rubio for political reasons. Then came the avalanche of
accusations: that I'm a Trump supporter (nope), that I'm a Huang fan (lol),
and my personal favorite, that I'm Chinese. Journalist Marcy Wheeler spoke for
those baffled that I'd say something so at odds with the mainstream reporting,
declaring me a member of the Matt Taibbi genus (wrong again).

That was just this week. Since launching this newsletter, I've done a lot of
stories nobody else wanted to touch. I tried to force a debate about the
gerontocracy with blunt headlines like "Our Dying Leaders." I wrote about my
visits from the FBI in hopes it would encourage others to do so as well. I
[warned](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/is-a-ground-war-with-iran-imminent)
that a ground invasion of Iran wouldn't happen -- despite countless headlines
to the contrary -- and that those of us opposed to the war should focus on the
air war actually happening.

These stories are often met with scorn at first but later accepted. I'm able
to do them for the simple reason that I don't have to worry about losing my
job. That's thanks to an army of people who have my back, sending me ten bucks
a month.

So who are my secret paymasters, the ones my haters keep asking about? You
alone are. Literally. There are no advertisers, no grants or foundation money,
no billionaire and (tragically) no trust fund.

There's no question that life for me would be easier if I just went along with
the mainstream. But I've never been able to join or conform. I just can't do
it. And I don't say that with pride. Independence can make for a pretty
isolating life.

And yet, for the first time in my life, I'm experiencing what I'm told is
called "belonging," thanks to the island of lovable misfits that's formed
around this newsletter.

My editor, [William Arkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Arkin), is a
fellow un-belonger who embodies paradoxes I never thought I'd find in one
person: populist but not stupid, deeply knowledgeable about the national
security world but not beholden to it, radical but not doctrinaire. Most
important, he's more than willing to stand up to me (😩) but also able to
listen.

It is an awesome and wholly undeserved gift I thought I'd never have, made
possible in part by the ten-dollar army.

During my [trip to the Galapagos](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/why-i-
disappeared) last December, I daydreamed about building something like those
islands: a remote place where strange forms of life could survive that the
dominant ecology everywhere else would wipe out. For me, that meant finding
people outside the social media supercontinent, which (as the Huang story
showed) forces everyone to pick a side. I wanted people who can still think
for themselves and stand up to the Washington juggernaut.

The comments section, which I read closely, is starting to look like that
island. There's Susan Becraft, whose warmth and encouragement genuinely help
me get through each week. She's in her 80s, as she's posted, but fully
supportive of my war on the gerontocracy.

"I'm 83, and I hope to live long enough to see all the bums, in both parties,
kicked to the curb," she writes in a comment I think about all the time.

It means a lot that my critique isn't taken as an attack on the elderly, but
on a specific type of Washington politician who's held office for way too
long. It's also a reminder of how much more intelligent people are than
they're given credit for. They aren't the demographic tribalists that
Washington would have you think.

There's Amelia, whose birthday is tomorrow (Happy Birthday!), who reminds me
that there are thoughtful people curious about national security beyond just
the dumbass war porn crowd. There's "Daas Yochid," who reminds me how nuanced
people's views can be. And there's Howie, whose surreal and profane jokes
remind me that there are other weirdos out there besides me.

One of my favorite things of all is the people who get annoyed, sometimes even
pissed off, at a story but show up the next day to read again. Despite our
transactional, audience-captured world of social media dance monkeys, it is a
beautiful reminder that there are still people who don't want to be pandered
to.

It's a weird and varied crew with one thing in common: they defy easy
classification. Like me.

If you're already a paid subscriber, thank you. You're the reason this is able
to exist -- literally. If you're not and you can swing it, it would mean the
world to us if you could [become a paid
subscriber](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/subscribe) or chip in to the

I'll see you in the comments.
